title: Classical Literature and the Science of Reading: When Two Worlds Collide
author: Classical Ed
summary: A classical educator and self-described Doug Lemov devotee reflects on how Lemov's new book, The Teach Like a Champion Guide to The Science of Reading, and his keynote at the Great Hearts National Symposium for Classical Education reignited her passion for reading instruction. Drawing on 11 years in the classroom, including six teaching first grade, she argues that the cognitive-science-backed Science of Reading movement and the classical tradition's commitment to great literature are not rivals but natural allies. She frames the central question of the essay as how rigorous, research-based decoding instruction can coexist with — and ultimately serve — the classical goal of cultivating wisdom and virtue through beautiful, substantive texts. The piece highlights the well-documented gap between time spent learning to read and time spent reading to learn, arguing schools must sustain phonics-level rigor well past the early grades. Ultimately she contends that decoding skill is only the foundation: students must also be drawn forward by 'Good and Beautiful' works so they grow into readers of Shakespeare and other classic literature, not just competent decoders.
points: Argues the Science of Reading and classical/Great Books education are complementary, not competing, movements in literacy instruction.
Uses Doug Lemov's Teach Like a Champion Guide to the Science of Reading as the catalyst for reconciling rigorous phonics-based decoding instruction with classical literary aims.
Highlights the real instructional problem: schools under-invest in sustained reading-skill development beyond the earliest grades, creating a gap between learning-to-read and reading-to-learn.

Frames the ultimate goal of reading instruction as producing not just capable decoders but readers formed by beauty and virtue — readers who can eventually engage Shakespeare and other canonical works.
Written from firsthand classroom experience (11 years teaching, including 6 in first grade), grounding the pedagogical argument in practice rather than abstract theory.
quotes: I preface this essay by stating that I am an unapologetic fan of Doug Lemov and his work, especially his book Teach Like a Champion.

In the fifteen years since I cracked open the pages of the first edition of Teach Like a Champion, I've appreciated the translation of research that Doug and his team provide to educators around the world.

This reignition began with a question: how does the research behind the Science of Reading and the beauty contained within classical literature not only co-exist but complement each other in cultivating wisdom and virtue?

After teaching first graders for the last 6 of my 11 years in the classroom, I knew the science of reading and classical texts could be simultaneously valued, however, I wrestled with two important questions.

It is essential to reiterate the conclusion based on their research that there is a large discrepancy in the time that students spend learning how to read as compared to the amount of time a student spends reading to learn.
We start strong in phonics and must ensure that the same intensity and commitment continue well beyond their elementary years so that students come to know the likes of Shakespeare.
